title: Java4Shell: GitLab helps find and remediate a critical Java flaw
summary:
GitLab has internally assessed the impact of Java4Shell, and concluded it is not exploitable in GitLab-managed infrastructure. Exploitation requires a specific combination of conditions, which we confirmed are not present in our production environment. A single component was found to contain the impacted bundle in its runtime environment, which we are proactively upgrading as a hardening measure.

On November 17, 2026, OpenJDK, the project that most Java runtimes are built from, fixed a memory corruption flaw known as Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938, CVSS 8.1) in the optimized java.util.Base64 decoding used on recent x86-64 CPUs. Web servers and frameworks routinely decode Base64 values from users, such as authentication headers and cookies, before the application sees the request. Researchers have demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution in the default configurations of several widely used Java products.

Upgrade Java to a fixed version now

To mitigate this issue, upgrade every Java runtime from 17.0.6 onward, including unsupported releases such as Java 18 and 24, to a build based on OpenJDK 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, or 27.0.1.1, or to your distribution’s patched package. If you can’t upgrade right away, turn off the vulnerable optimization with the -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics JVM option.

Here are fixed builds and packages as of November 19:

Sources: the OpenJDK advisory, vendors’ release pages, and the Ubuntu, Debian, Alpine, and Red Hat security trackers, as of November 19, 2026.

How you apply the upgrade depends on where Java runs:

  1. Containers with a floating tag, such as amazoncorretto:21: Rebuild the image so it pulls the latest base image, then redeploy.
  2. Containers with a pinned tag: Change the tag to a fixed version, then redeploy.
  3. Hosts: Upgrade the package, then restart every Java process.

For containers, check that the new base image ships a fixed version. As of November 19, eclipse-temurin:21 and the images built on it, such as tomcat, still don't, so they need the workaround below until they do.

If you can’t upgrade yet, turn off the vulnerable optimization

Set the -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics JVM option, and restart every Java process for it to take effect. Base64 decoding will then use the regular version, which doesn’t have the flaw, and is only slightly slower.

To apply it to every JVM a container starts, add it to the JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS environment variable, keeping any value already set. In a shell script, such as the container’s entrypoint, add this line of code:

export JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="${JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS:+$JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS }-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics"

To confirm the option is set, run java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics in the container, which should print false.

Locate Java projects across your GitLab groups

Any project that runs Java needs a fixed version, including the ones that are easy to forget, such as a CI tool, a build server, or a product that bundles its own JDK. Finding them takes two views: a static search of what your repositories declare and your images contain, and a runtime inventory of what actually runs. GitLab covers the static view with three features: container scanning, GitLab Orbit, and a language filter. Use them in this order.

1. Container scanning

Container scanning reports vulnerabilities in operating system packages, so it finds Java installed with apt, apk, or dnf. It reports the CVE once the CVE reaches the advisories in the scanner’s vulnerability database. To turn it on for a project, add the template to .gitlab-ci.yml:

include:  
  - template: Security/Container-Scanning.gitlab-ci.yml  
   
container_scanning:  
  variables:  
    # Experimental, Ultimate only: also reports runtimes not installed by a package manager  
    CS_BINARY_SCAN: "true"

You can also use a group-level scan execution policy to turn container scanning on for every project in a group at once. Once the policy is on, the next pipeline in each project runs container scanning. After the scan completes, review the default branch’s results in the Vulnerability Report.

You can also set up merge request approval policies with container scanning. If a code change contains Java4Shell, the policy blocks the merge until the selected approvers approve it.

In addition, turn on CS_BINARY_SCAN to find Java runtimes that no package manager installed, such as the JDK archive the eclipse-temurin images unpack or a JDK bundled in an application. The default scan can’t see them because they have no package record. The binary scan identifies them and reports Java4Shell.

2. GitLab Orbit

GitLab Orbit indexes your projects, pipelines, security findings, and source code, including Java, into a context graph you can query. You can ask an agent to review an entire group. With Orbit enabled on the top-level group, an agent can list every project that contains Java code, including the projects that JDK container scanning misses. You can also ask Orbit which projects have open findings for CVE-2026-114938 once scans have run. Orbit indexes the default branch only and is in beta for Premium and Ultimate on GitLab.com and GitLab Self-Managed.

3. Projects by language

GitLab detects the languages in each project’s default branch, so a language filter lists every project that contains Java or Kotlin code, one row per project, whatever build tool it uses. Open Explore > Projects and filter by language, then again for Kotlin. Alternatively, you can get the list through the REST API:

GET /groups//projects?with_programming_language=Java&include_subgroups=true

4. Compare with your runtime inventory

Container scanning, Orbit, and the language filter show what your projects declare and build, but Java can also run outside your GitLab projects. It often runs in application servers and products installed on hosts by hand, in CI runners and build servers, or in containers that still run in clusters without an active pipeline.

Compare the static results with an inventory of your running workloads from your configuration management (Ansible, Puppet, Chef, etc.), cloud, or VM inventory tools. Note which hosts run on affected x86-64 CPUs. For Kubernetes, operational container scanning scans the images that run in your clusters. It uses the same package-only detection as the container scanning in Step 1. Treat every Java runtime that appears in only one of the two views as a gap to investigate.

Remediate at scale with GitLab Duo Agent Platform

GitLab Duo can run the discovery steps above for you: pass it the list of projects filtered by language, or ask it to find them through Orbit. From there, let agents do the repetitive work, while keeping humans in the loop to review and merge.

To have agents open the fixes for every affected project:

  1. Set up a flow trigger on the Assign event, so the Developer Flow starts when someone assigns an issue.
  2. Turn on automatic reviews with the Code Review Flow to get a first review that follows your custom review instructions.
  3. Use Agentic Chat to create an epic with one issue per affected project, and assign the Developer Flow to each. The flow opens a merge request that updates the base image tag or package to a fixed version, or, where no fixed image exists yet, sets -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics in JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS.

title: Rotate a leaked GitLab token and let GitLab Duo fix the code
summary:
Secret detection alerts you when an active personal access token (PAT) is exposed in your default branch. Acting on that finding is harder: revoking the token breaks dependent pipelines, and replacing it safely takes several manual steps. While the finding waits in your vulnerability report, the token stays live.

Starting in GitLab 19.6 in beta for GitLab Ultimate, you can remediate a leaked GitLab PAT directly from the vulnerability page. Select Rotate and fix, and GitLab revokes the token, stores a replacement in GitLab Secrets Manager, and uses GitLab Duo Agent Platform to open a merge request (MR) to update your CI/CD jobs. You review and merge the MR. GitLab never exposes the new token value to you or your agents.

Why leaked tokens stay active after detection

Imagine that secret detection flags an active PAT in deploy.sh:

export GITLAB_TOKEN="glpat-..."

Fixing this manually requires tracking down the token's owner, revoking it, generating a replacement with matching scopes, storing it securely, and opening MRs to update your scripts and CI/CD jobs.

Because this process is tedious, remediations often stall or go wrong:

  • The finding ages: Nobody wants to break the pipeline, so the finding sits in the vulnerability report while the token remains active.
  • The fix stops halfway: Someone revokes the token immediately, breaking the build. In a rush to recover, they paste a replacement into a less secure CI/CD variable.
  • The new token leaks: Someone shares the replacement token in a chat thread so a teammate can configure it.

In the gap between detected and rotated, the token still works for anyone who can read the repository.

Rotate and fix in a snap

The Rotate and fix function closes this gap by combining secret detection and validity checks, GitLab Secrets Manager, and GitLab Duo Agent Platform.

When you open an active PAT finding and select AI actions > Fix with AI > Rotate and fix, GitLab:

  1. Revokes the leaked token and creates a replacement with the same name, scopes, and duration (reset from the rotation date).
  2. Stores the new value as a project secret in Secrets Manager, available to all branches and environments.
  3. Marks the token as inactive on the vulnerability.
  4. Starts a GitLab Duo Developer Flow session, which opens an MR to remove the hardcoded token and configure your CI/CD jobs to read the secret.

You review the MR, merge it, and resolve the vulnerability.

Update the code without exposing the new token

Rotation finishes before the agent starts, so GitLab Duo never sees the new token. By the time GitLab Duo reads the file to remove the hardcoded credential, the value is revoked and the replacement is safely stored in Secrets Manager. The agent receives only the vulnerability and its file location, the new secret's name, and your username so it can assign the MR to you. GitLab Duo then updates your pipeline configuration:

deploy:
  secrets:
    GITLAB_TOKEN:
      gitlab_secrets_manager:
        name: ROTATED_GITLAB_TOKEN_123
      file: false
  script:
    - ./deploy.sh

Your script continues using GITLAB_TOKEN, which Secrets Manager injects at runtime.

What to know before you implement

  • Availability: This beta feature requires GitLab Ultimate 19.6 or later. It is enabled by default on GitLab.com, available behind the secrets_manager_pat_rotation feature flag on GitLab Self-Managed, and not yet available on GitLab Dedicated.
  • Supported secret types: Rotation supports GitLab PATs, including fine-grained PATs. It doesn't yet cover other secrets that secret detection finds, such as cloud provider keys.
  • Immediate and irreversible: The leaked token stops working right away, and you can't undo the rotation. Scripts outside GitLab CI/CD and jobs in other projects that used the old token need a new token, because the new secret is scoped only to the current project and its raw value cannot be retrieved.
  • Ownership rules: On GitLab.com, you can rotate only your own tokens. On GitLab Self-Managed, administrators can also rotate tokens belonging to other users.
  • Independent of AI: If the GitLab Duo session cannot start, GitLab still rotates the old token and stores the replacement so you can update the code manually.

For role requirements, required settings, and step-by-step instructions, see the leaked token rotation documentation.

Automate rotation across a group

Rotating tokens one by one doesn't scale across large organizations. Rotate and fix makes two API calls: the projectSecretCreateFromLeakedToken GraphQL mutation, which rotates the token and stores the secret, and a request that starts the GitLab Duo Developer Flow.

We packaged both calls into leaked-token-rotation-automation, a dependency-free Python CLI and CI/CD component that batch-rotates tokens across an entire group:

  • Active vulnerability findings: Rotates active leaked PATs across your group's repositories and opens an MR for each finding. On GitLab.com, it rotates your own tokens and lists other users' tokens in the report for follow-up. On GitLab Self-Managed, an administrator can rotate every user's tokens.
  • Tokens in CI/CD variables: Secret detection doesn't scan project CI/CD variables, and any project Maintainer can read a variable that isn't hidden. The tool finds GitLab PATs in those variables, rotates them, and stores the new values in Secrets Manager. If any jobs use the variable, GitLab Duo opens an MR to update them. Each token rotates itself using its own api or self_rotate scope, so this command also works on tokens that belong to other users. It skips group, instance, file-type, and hidden variables.

Every run defaults to dry-run mode (pass --apply to execute), stops after 10 rotations (configurable with --limit), and never includes token values in reports. See the project README for installation instructions, CI/CD component usage, and required token scopes.

Getting started

To try this out, you need GitLab Ultimate, GitLab Duo Agent Platform, and Secrets Manager, which you can evaluate with a free 30-day trial. Each rotation consumes GitLab Credits for the Developer Flow session and for the stored secret and each CI/CD job that reads it.

  1. Review the prerequisites and troubleshooting guide to ensure validity checks and Developer Flow are enabled. On GitLab Self-Managed, also enable the secrets_manager_pat_rotation feature flag.
  2. Open an active PAT finding in your vulnerability report, select AI actions > Fix with AI > Rotate and fix, and review the resulting merge request.
  3. Run the leaked-token-rotation-automation tool in dry-run mode to preview which tokens you can rotate across your group.

What's next

We’re building a migration workflow into GitLab that imports sensitive CI/CD variables into GitLab Secrets Manager, with no values to re-enter. GitLab will automatically find variables that look like credentials and apply default access policies to the ones you choose to migrate. GitLab Duo will then open a merge request that updates your pipeline configuration, so all you have to do is review and merge.

title: Turn Slack conversations into trusted software, faster
summary:
Most software starts as a conversation: a customer requests a new capability, a product manager weighs it against the roadmap, an engineer checks feasibility, and a security lead asks what it touches.

Then someone has to turn it into work. They reread the thread, retype the decisions into an issue, and hope they didn’t miss an important detail buried in a reply. The conversation moves fast; the handoff between both teams and tools is where it slows.

AI agents are uniquely equipped for that handoff: reading a long, many-voiced discussion and turning it into structured work. That leaves people free to collaborate while agents produce the output.

GitLab for Slack now adds agentic capabilities and is generally available for GitLab.com users in GitLab 19.6, with support for GitLab Self-Managed and GitLab Dedicated to follow. Mention @GitLab in a thread in your team's channels, and the agent reads the conversation, finds what already exists, turns decisions into tracked work, and starts the agent flows that carry it to production. Work starts in Slack and lands in GitLab, where it's governed, tracked, and delivered.

"Teams make decisions in Slack every day, and the best agents are the ones that can act on that context. GitLab for Slack lets agents read the conversation, take action across the software lifecycle in GitLab, and bring the results back to the thread. Teams can go from a quick discussion to planned, reviewed, and shipped work without switching tools."

– Katie Steigman, Vice President Product Management, Slack

Slack is the front door, GitLab does the work

GitLab for Slack connects the interface where your team discusses the work to the platform where your software ships. Your team’s conversation in Slack itself becomes the agent's input, so no decision gets lost between the thread and the first commit.

The agent also looks beyond the thread. When you mention @GitLab, it can read the messages in the channel where you mentioned it, so its response reflects the whole discussion and not only the replies under one message. You can also ask it to catch you up first, for example: “@GitLab, summarize #channel for me.”

It works in both directions. GitLab context (what's been built, what's tracked, whether a merge request is ready, etc.) also shows up in the conversation. The conversation becomes issues, merge requests, and running agent flows, with results posted back to the thread.

If your team already uses the GitLab for Slack app on GitLab.com, reinstall it today to add these agent capabilities. There's nothing new to learn; you just mention @GitLab.

Use it where your team works

Debate it in the channel. Draft it in your DM. GitLab for Slack works in both places:

  • Public and private channels: Bring the agent into team discussions and turn decisions into tracked work where everyone can see it.
  • Your own DM: Get a private space to ask questions, check on a merge request, or draft an issue before you share anything with the team.

One thread, every role

GitLab for Slack works for everyone who shapes the work, including people who never write code:

  • Product managers turn a decision into scoped work before the meeting ends.
  • Designers send their notes straight to the people and agents doing the work.
  • Sales and customer teams bring a customer request into a team channel and follow it to production.
  • Security and platform teams confirm agent work passes review before it ships.
  • Engineers check what exists before building it again, without leaving the conversation.

Watch GitLab for Slack in action:

Governed from the first mention

An agent that acts from a chat thread is only useful if you can trust what it does. The conversation happens in Slack; the work and every control stay in GitLab.

  • Agents act only when asked. In channels, GitLab acts only when someone mentions @GitLab. In your own DM, it answers you and only you.
  • Internal conversations only. GitLab for Slack doesn't run in external (Slack Connect) channels, so project context isn't exposed to people outside your organization.
  • Requests run as you. Each request uses the requester's linked GitLab account, scoped to their existing permissions. If you don't have access to a project in GitLab, the agent can't access it for you in Slack.
  • Context stays in scope. The agent reads the surrounding context only from the channel where it was mentioned. Anything it does in GitLab still follows your permissions.
  • Actions are on the record. Each request creates an agent session in GitLab. Merge requests go through the same reviews, approval rules, and audit trail as any other change.
  • Costs stay visible. Usage draws from your GitLab Credits, so admins can track and cap it like any other agent work.

This is the model behind GitLab's governed software factory: agents speed up the work, and source control, security, and governance keep it trustworthy. Slack is one more way into that factory, not a way around it.

Get started

GitLab for Slack is now generally available on GitLab.com — just reinstall the GitLab for Slack app to get the new capabilities. Support for GitLab Self-Managed and GitLab Dedicated will follow in an upcoming release.

Help us shape what's next

We have a lot more planned for GitLab for Slack, and we want your feedback to guide it. Every agent response in Slack includes a thumbs up/down button, so you can tell us what worked and what didn't without leaving the thread.

title: Keep recurring work moving with scheduled automations
summary:
Every engineering team has work that needs regular attention, like triaging new issues or investigating incidents. Among DevSecOps professionals using AI tools, 43% say automating repetitive tasks has created the most efficiency, according to GitLab’s Global DevSecOps report. But agents still rely on a human to kick off the workflow or an event trigger to fire, and without a record of what ran and why, no one can trace how the work got done.

With scheduled automations, in beta in GitLab 19.6, flows in GitLab Duo Agent Platform handle routine tasks on a schedule your team sets and keep a history of what ran. Scheduled automations are a building block of the governed software factory, where agents and flows work autonomously within controls set by your team.

Put routine work on a schedule

Relying on a person or an event to start automated work limits efficiency gains and makes timing unpredictable. When the person responsible is out, the work waits, and when there’s no event, it never starts. Scheduled automations give routine work a dependable rhythm.

You can already run event-based automations in GitLab Duo Agent Platform, triggered by activities like a merge request or a mention in a comment. Scheduled automations start the work on a recurring schedule, with no event needed. Describe the task in plain language, set the cadence once, and the automation runs on its own at the times you choose, with run counts and success rates your team can review.

Triage new issues daily to keep your backlog organized, or schedule a flow to check CI health incidents every hour and comment with the likely root cause, so the investigation is underway before anyone opens the issue.

You can set a schedule from every 15 minutes to every month, at the time of day and in the timezone that meets the needs of your group. Because automations in GitLab drive the work your whole team depends on, each one runs at the project level.

See how to schedule an automation, from describing the task to reviewing its first run:

Control and transparency for every run

As agents take on more of the work around your code, teams need to know which agent acted, what permissions it had, and what it did. Without a verifiable identity and a record of every change, no one can say which agent made a change or why it ran, and every review or audit starts with reconstruction. It’s hard to scale agentic work when you can’t see what agents or flows already did.

Scheduled automations offer the controls a team needs to trust what runs on its own. Each automation runs as a dedicated service account with scoped permissions, so your team can tell agent work from human work in the audit events. Audit events also record changes to every automation, so your team knows what ran, what happened, and who changed it.

A redesigned Automations page, previously labeled Triggers, brings scheduled and event-based automations together in one place, with run volume, success rate, and session details for each, so your team can see details of what ran and what happened. If a run fails, the page shows the reason, and you can open the session to see exactly what the agent did.

A foundation of the governed software factory

The governed software factory is a connected system for moving software from idea to production under your organization’s own policy and standards, with an evidence chain that records how every change got there.

Scheduled automations add a critical piece to that foundation by automating work into the factory on a regular basis. A weekly scan for vulnerabilities can create work items for the factory to act on, and every automation runs as its own service account with scoped permissions, so its actions stay easy to identify.

Scheduling the right work keeps the factory moving, saves your team time, and leaves a record they can trust. Creating one of these automations is a good place to start:

  • CI health investigation - An hourly check of open incidents that comments with the likely root cause, so the investigation is underway before anyone opens the issue.
  • Issue triage - A morning review of new issues that decides whether each is a bug or a feature and adds a label, so the backlog stays organized.
  • Stale work report - A weekly report that lists the open issues with no activity in the last 30 days in a new issue, so stuck work gets a second look.
  • Duplicate spotting - A daily check of new issues that comments with any open issues that look like the same request, so duplicates get linked before anyone triages them twice.
  • Weekly digest - A Friday summary of what closed and merged that week, written in plain language for people outside engineering and posted as a new issue, so stakeholders know what shipped without reading MR titles.

Try scheduled automations today

Scheduled automations are available now in beta in GitLab 19.6. Like other flows on GitLab Duo Agent Platform, scheduled automations use GitLab Credits. To try one, turn on experimental and beta features, choose a routine your team repeats, like one of the recommendations above, and put it on a schedule.

If you’re new to GitLab Duo Agent Platform, start a free trial. Already on Premium or Ultimate? Turn on Duo Agent Platform and use the GitLab Credits included with your subscription.

title: Cut your vulnerability backlog with agentic remediation
summary:
Vulnerability backlogs are growing faster than teams can clear them. AI writes more code and finds more flaws, while fixes still move at human speed. NIST’s National Vulnerability Database has already published twice as many CVEs in 2026 as in all of 2025, and ceased enriching most CVEs this past April.

Compounding the problem, a finding that looks safe to defer may not stay that way. Attackers now use AI to find and exploit flaws in hours, even those long written off as theoretical. In October, frontier models uncovered PHP2Shell, a pair of unauthenticated remote code execution bugs in PHP that had been dismissed as unexploitable in 2012.

Discovery and exploitation now run at machine speed. To keep up, defenders need agentic security tools that detect and remediate vulnerabilities with minimal manual effort while leaving teams in full control.

GitLab 19.6 helps teams shrink their security findings backlog. Security managers can now turn on agentic triage and remediation across entire groups of projects without scripting against the API. A new agentic flow adds exploitability context to static application security testing (SAST) findings, so teams can prioritize the ones that pose real risk. Security leaders can then track the results on a new mean time to remediation (MTTR) chart.

Find and fix faster with agentic security

GitLab 19.6 builds on a platform that finds and fixes vulnerabilities with agentic security. GitLab Duo security agents use frontier AI reasoning to examine your codebase and every merge request for the logic flaws scanners miss, while built-in scanners catch known vulnerabilities from source to runtime. Agents filter out false positives before they reach a developer's queue, then help teams prioritize the rest by severity, exploitability, reachability, and blast radius. GitLab Orbit, our native knowledge graph, grounds that reasoning in the live state of your system.

For confirmed findings, an agent writes a fix, opens a merge request, and triggers the pipeline to rerun tests and scans. If anything fails, the agent reads the logs, revises the fix, and retests. Developers review a ready-to-merge fix with the agent's rationale and confidence score. That fix goes through the same approvals as any other change, and neither developers nor agents can bypass them. Remediation keeps pace with discovery, and the backlog shrinks.

GitLab 19.6 advances agentic remediation

GitLab 19.6 puts agents to work across more of that backlog. It extends agentic triage and remediation to more projects, adds exploitability context to SAST findings, and charts MTTR.

Turn on agents across many projects

Agents shrink the backlog only where they run, and turning them on one project at a time doesn't scale to thousands. Automated triage and remediation (ATR) profiles let security managers turn on agentic flows across many projects at once. In the first week after ATR profiles became accessible via API, one customer applied them to 136 projects, saving significant time.

A single profile turns on flows like false-positive detection, risk contextualization, and vulnerability resolution. Security managers choose one of three presets — Conservative, Standard, or Proactive — to set which severity levels each flow addresses and whether it runs automatically or only on demand.

Until now, applying an ATR profile required writing a script. In 19.6, security managers select projects by group or attribute from the Security Inventory or the security configuration page, choose a profile, and apply it. Afterward, Security Inventory shows which projects have a flow turned on, alongside their scanner coverage.


ATR profiles are available to GitLab Ultimate customers on all GitLab offerings. To use them, follow the ATR profile setup steps.

Assess the exploitability of SAST findings with Vulnerability Context Flow

Without exposure context, a SAST finding in an isolated internal service looks as urgent as the same finding in a public-facing service that handles sensitive data.

Vulnerability Context Flow identifies and analyzes the affected service, even in a monorepo, and adds a risk table to the SAST finding. The table shows whether exploiting the flaw requires authentication or elevated authorization, whether the service handles sensitive data, and whether it is exposed to untrusted input. Teams can then rank the backlog by exploitability as well as severity.


Vulnerability Context Flow is in beta for GitLab Ultimate customers on all GitLab offerings in 19.6. To turn it on, follow the Vulnerability Context Flow setup.

See mean time to remediation at a glance

Security leaders track MTTR to understand how long vulnerabilities stay open and whether that window is shrinking. The security dashboard now charts weekly MTTR for findings in first-party code and third-party dependencies, at the project, group, and organization level. The chart shows MTTR alongside the number of vulnerabilities fixed each week. You can group results by severity or scan type and filter by project.


The chart includes vulnerabilities that have been resolved or are no longer detected, and excludes dismissed ones. To keep longstanding findings from distorting the trend, each week counts only vulnerabilities detected in the 90 days before that week began.

The MTTR chart is on by default for GitLab Ultimate customers in 19.6. To check the prerequisites, see the security dashboard documentation.

Turn on Business Logic Security Analyzer, with Claude Mythos 5.2 on request

GitLab Ultimate customers on GitLab.com can now turn on Business Logic Security Analyzer (BLSA) themselves. BLSA scans your repository the way a security engineer would, uncovering broken ownership logic, missing authorization checks, and multi-step abuse paths.

BLSA is in beta for GitLab Ultimate customers in 19.6. On GitLab.com, turn it on by following the business logic scanning setup. On GitLab Self-Managed and GitLab Dedicated, contact us for access. To power BLSA with Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5.2, contact your account team.

Get started with agentic remediation in GitLab 19.6

Apply an automated triage and remediation profile to a project with a large backlog, and turn on Vulnerability Context Flow to rank the remaining SAST findings by exploitability. In the coming weeks, track the results on the MTTR chart. To catch the flaws scanners miss, turn on Business Logic Security Analyzer, now available via self-service on GitLab.com.

These features require GitLab Ultimate. Try GitLab Ultimate for free to test agentic security on your own projects.

title: The best way to use your coding agents with GitLab
summary:
Say you and your team already use Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Devin, or OpenCode to write code. Maybe even more than one of them.

What happens next depends on everyone’s personal setup.

Some have their agent review changes, watch CI pipelines and security checks, with a different approach to follow up when something breaks. Others do it by hand. When those steps depend on each engineer’s setup, skill, or time to follow up, even changes in the same project move at different speeds and get different levels of scrutiny.

We paired each one of these coding agents to create a recommended configuration that makes your best engineering practices the default for the whole team.

  • One bar for every change. You set security, architecture, and engineering standards once in GitLab. Duo reviews changes against your review instructions, and GitLab enforces required pipelines, security checks, and approvals before merge, whether a coding agent or a person wrote the change.
  • Give agents the context they need. Duo can work from the repository, merge request discussion, CI logs, and scanner results. Your team doesn’t have to piece that context back together every time work moves between tools or people.
  • Delegation without handing over keys. Composite identity ties every agent action to the agent and the person who started it, and limits access to what both are allowed to do.
  • Leave a record the next engineer can use. Reviews, pipeline results, and approvals stay with the merge request. A pipeline fix can link back to its Duo session. Anyone picking up the work can see what ran and what still needs attention without reconstructing someone else’s agent conversation.
  • Your models, your cloud. Pick the model for each agentic flow from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google or open-weight providers, and change it when a better one ships.

What’s new

Your coding agent writes the code. GitLab Duo does the work that starts at the merge request and follows through to deployment.

You can now set up code review, pipeline repair, and security triage together from your coding session. The GitLab Duo setup skill connects your agent to GitLab and configures automatic review and failed-pipeline repair. On the Ultimate tier, you can also opt in to security triage and remediation. The skill tells you what, if anything, still needs your attention.

Once configured, the work keeps running in GitLab even if you close your editor. When you come back, the optional MR follow-up skill checks what’s already running and brings review and pipeline feedback back into your coding session.

For a deep dive on how to use our new skills, please see our detailed guide here.

What you and your team get

Give every eligible MR a separate review for 25¢

Your coding agent can check its own work before it pushes. Duo gives the change a second look when the MR is marked ready and posts feedback on the diff. A review costs a flat $0.25 at list price, so 1,000 reviews cost $250. Anthropic's Code Review averages $15–$25 a review, so the same volume would cost $15,000 or more. That makes a first pass practical even for routine changes.

Then ask your agent to read the comments, fix the ones you agree with, and reply on each thread.

Turn security findings into fixes you can verify

On Ultimate, Duo flags likely false positives from static application security testing and secret detection and opens MRs with fixes for eligible SAST findings, usually about 10 minutes after a scan. Your team gets a proposed change it can test, scan, and review under the same rules as any other change.

Start investigating when CI goes red

When a pipeline fails, an automation starts Fix CI/CD Pipeline while you're on to something else, and links the session on the MR. Duo suggests a change, opens a fix MR, or explains what it found if it can't propose a reliable fix. The fix still has to pass CI. While Duo works on the fix on GitLab, your coding harness can also collaborate with Duo to review the proposed fix, commit a change to the MR, and watch for the pipeline to pass.

Take an MR to merge, with policy-based approvals

The MR follow-up skill checks the review threads, failed jobs, and conflicts on an MR, and works through them from your agent. Your agent can resolve a merge conflict in your checkout, or hand it to the Developer flow to resolve in GitLab. The skill stops when only approvals are left.

Then your approval rules decide what merges, for agent changes and people alike. Approval policies can require a person to approve every MR, or add approvers when a scan finds a vulnerability. Pipeline execution policies make required jobs run. Tool approval guardrails can make an agent ask a person before a sensitive action. Tool calls that go through GitLab’s MCP server can be viewed in Audit events when storage is enabled. If you let Duo approve MRs, its approval doesn't count toward required approvals.

Hand an issue to GitLab Duo and get back a merge request

Ask your agent to hand an assigned issue to the Developer flow. The flow runs in GitLab, reads the issue and the repository, writes the change, and opens an MR in your name. You keep working locally, and nobody has to copy the issue and the code history into a prompt.

How to get started

Paste this into your coding agent:


Install the skills from https://gitlab.com/gitlab-da/projects/agentic-eng-config and run gitlab-duo-setup for my GitLab group. Show me the plan before you change anything.

Your agent checks what's already on and shows one plan. Nothing changes until you approve it. Someone with the Owner role can set up the whole GitLab group. A person with a Maintainer role can start with one GitLab project.

Then try it on real work:

  • "Summarize the Duo feedback on MR !42. Which findings would you address, and what would you change?"
  • "Did Duo propose a fix for the failed pipeline on MR !42? Show me the diff and why it should fix the failure."
  • "Take MR !42 through to merge."
  • "Find my assigned issues in . Hand the best-scoped one to the Duo Developer flow."

If you are new to Duo Agent Platform and GitLab Ultimate, you can start a free trial.

title: GitLab Transcend Hackathon: Meet the 'Life After Code' winners
summary:
Code generation is the easy part now. The hard part is everything that comes after it: getting software from a working change to running in production. That’s the problem we put to the community in the Transcend Hackathon: “Life after code, the path to production at the speed of imagination”.

The hackathon, which ran during October, challenged participants to build agents and flows on GitLab Duo Agent Platform that can take over the work after the code is written. They also had to decide how much control to hand the agents, from approving every step to making them completely autonomous. More than 3,300 developers registered and 783 projects were submitted.

The winning projects show how far agents and flows can go after code generation. A pharmacy app bug reported simply by shaking a phone was fixed and shipped in 18 minutes with no human in the middle. A teacher's email became a 3D-printable math graph a blind student could read by touch. A flow applied to a benefits software app helped detect payment miscalculations based on a won appeal. What these projects share: Agents do the reading, writing, and routing, while automated checks and people make the final calls.

The winners

The prize pool was $45,000 across nine categories, with each project eligible for one path prize and one special prize. You can find the full field in the project gallery.

Path A: Start Fresh

New projects built from scratch on GitLab

Best Assisted Agent ($4,000): Aftermath

Aftermath by Ahadi Cyizere answers the question scanners can't: When a hijacked npm package is disclosed, had it already run in last week's CI? A custom GitLab Duo flow with three subagents traces past CI jobs and the credentials each job could reach. A person signs off on the scope of the investigation, then on the containment plan, and finally closes the incident once CI has rotated only the exposed keys and deleted the affected images, and proof is attached.

Best Supervised Agent ($4,000): Lookback

Lookback by Ujwal Suresh Vanjare and Arpita Madhukar Kalburgi starts from a won appeal. When benefits software gets the rules wrong for one person, a custom GitLab Duo flow triages the decision, reproduces the error with a failing test, and opens a fix merge request. After a person merges it, plain code replays past decisions to find every other household the bug affected and works out what each is owed. In the demo run, the replay found 413 underpaid households, and the amounts owed were published as a batch for the agency to pay.

Best Hands-Off Agent ($5,000): ShakeFix

ShakeFix by Venkatesh Devale turns a phone shake into a production fix. A user of a pharmacy app shakes her phone and says what went wrong, and a GitLab Duo flow with four agents writes a failing test, fixes the bug, and checks the fix against production behavior side by side before it merges and deploys. In the team's live run, that process took just 18 minutes and 34 seconds with no human touches.

Path B: Bring Your Own

Existing open source projects with agent-driven automation added and deployed on GitLab

Best Assisted Agent ($4,000): Unstuck

Unstuck by Aryan Shah and Riken Shah finishes the dependency upgrades that bots start but can't complete. A bot bumps a version number, but it can't read the release notes, fix what breaks, or decide what happens when behavior changes. Two custom GitLab Duo flows plan an upgrade campaign and carry it out one merge request at a time, quoting the release note behind every code change and stopping to ask a person when behavior would change. A daily monitor opens the next campaign when a new advisory appears. On doccano, an open source annotation tool stuck on an unsupported Django version with 80 known advisories, the campaign took the project to zero advisories and Django 5.2 in six reviewed merge requests.

Best Supervised Agent ($4,000): CodeTinder

CodeTinder by Jason Yu is built on a simple idea: review less code, teach agents more. On each merge request, a GitLab Duo agent picks one function and writes variants that pass the tests, and users swipe through the variants on their phone. The swipes update a versioned principles doc in the repo, which every agent reads, and an agent rewrites the rest of the merge request to match the updated doc.

Best Hands-off Agent ($5,000): Locus

Locus by Ahammad Shawki, Nourin Richi, and Mohammad Ashfaqul Hasan, built on the open source JSCAD library, lets a math teacher email a function in plain words and get back a tactile graph for a blind student. GitLab Duo agents design a raised-line graph with braille labels, check it against research-based touch rules for how fingertips read raised lines and braille, correct their own mistakes, publish the result on Google Cloud, send the print files to the teacher, and order the print graph. The agents can't mark their own work as ready to print; a graph is released only when it passes the touch rules.

Special prizes

The Most Stages Covered prize goes to the projects that touch the most of the nine DevSecOps lifecycle stages: Plan, Create, Verify, Package, Secure, Release, Configure, Monitor, and Govern. There is one winner from each path.

Most Stages Covered, Start Fresh ($5,000): Stale

Stale by Diptarka Nandi, Harshit Anand, Abhinav Kumar, and Ashutosh Pandey re-checks "safe to ship" verdicts when the world changes, not just when code does. A scheduled pipeline watches live feeds, such as a root certificate being distrusted, and opens an issue for a GitLab Duo flow that writes the fix. CI proves the fix, and a canary release probes it before traffic moves. It maps every lifecycle stage to a real pipeline job.

Most Stages Covered, Bring Your Own ($5,000): Earned Autonomy

Earned Autonomy by Shivansh Kalra gives every merge request on the FastAPI full-stack template its own level of autonomy, from hands-off to blocked, based on evidence. Five GitLab Duo agents handle planning, triage, infrastructure review, routing, and rollback, and can only ever raise the risk score. In one run, a vulnerable dependency went from advisory to a fixed production deploy in 35 minutes with no human step. In another, a bad release was rolled back in 3.3 seconds.

Most Environmentally Impactful ($5,000): Memory Lane

Memory Lane by Oliver McBride helps care-home coordinators build reminiscence sessions for residents with dementia. A coordinator files a plain-English issue, and three GitLab Duo flows carry it through safety review, CI/CD, and Cloud Run to production. The team measured the carbon cost of each shipped request using the Software Carbon Intensity spec, then re-engineered the pipeline to build once and skip needless runs. That cut CI-per-shipped requests by 48%.

Most Creative ($4,000): CodeTinder

CodeTinder wins in this category, too. Swiping to teach agents your taste in code was the highest-scoring idea across both paths.

What we learned

The winners kept agents on a short leash and still got a lot out of them. Agents handled the reading, writing, and routing: working out what an upgrade would break, tracing a bug to the line of code behind it, and handing the work to the next step. Automated checks like tests and CI decide whether each step passes, and, in most projects, a person signs off before anything risky ships. The winners also aimed their agents at problems outside typical software work, including pharmacy apps, benefits systems, care homes, and blind students’ classrooms.

Keep building

To everyone who entered, thank you. Thank you also to our judges: Bill Staples, Missy Davies, Mattias Michaux, Lee Tickett, Rajesh Agadi, Luca Chun Lun Lit, Alan Zhang, Jackson Dolphin, and Arianna Haradon.

If you'd like to experiment with GitLab Duo Agent Platform and contribute to GitLab itself, sign up at contributors.gitlab.com to get a personalized onboarding issue and an issue finder to help you pick your first contribution.

Aftermath by Ahadi Cyizere answers the question scanners can't: When a hijacked npm package is disclosed, had it already run in last week's CI? A custom GitLab Duo flow with three subagents traces past CI jobs and the credentials each job could reach. A person signs off on the scope of the investigation, then on the containment plan, and finally closes the incident once CI has rotated only the exposed keys and deleted the affected images, and proof is attached.

Best Supervised Agent ($4,000): Lookback

Lookback by Ujwal Suresh Vanjare and Arpita Madhukar Kalburgi starts from a won appeal. When benefits software gets the rules wrong for one person, a custom GitLab Duo flow triages the decision, reproduces the error with a failing test, and opens a fix merge request. Existing open source projects with agent-driven automation added and deployed on GitLab

The swipes update a versioned principles doc in the repo, which every agent reads, and an agent rewrites the rest of the merge request to match the updated doc.

Locus by Ahammad Shawki, Nourin Richi, and Mohammad Ashfaqul Hasan, built on the open source JSCAD library, lets a math teacher email a function in plain words and get back a tactile graph for a blind student. GitLab Duo agents design a raised-line graph with braille labels, check it against research-based touch rules for how fingertips read raised lines and braille, correct their own mistakes, publish the result on Google Cloud, send the print files to the teacher, and order the print graph. The agents can't mark their own work as ready to print; a graph is released only when it passes the touch rules.

Special prizes

The Most Stages Covered prize goes to the projects that touch the most of the nine DevSecOps lifecycle stages: Plan, Create, Verify, Package, Secure, Release, Configure, Monitor, and Govern. There is one winner from each path.

Most Stages Covered, Start Fresh ($5,000): Stale

Stale by Diptarka Nandi, Harshit Anand, Abhinav Kumar, and Ashutosh Pandey re-checks "safe to ship" verdicts when the world changes, not just when code does. A scheduled pipeline watches live feeds, such as a root certificate being distrusted, and opens an issue for a GitLab Duo flow that writes the fix. CI proves the fix, and a canary release probes it before traffic moves. It maps every lifecycle stage to a real pipeline job.

Most Stages Covered, Bring Your Own ($5,000): Earned Autonomy

Earned Autonomy by Shivansh Kalra gives every merge request on the FastAPI full-stack template its own level of autonomy, from hands-off to blocked, based on evidence. Five GitLab Duo agents handle planning, triage, infrastructure review, routing, and rollback, and can only ever raise the risk score. In one run, a vulnerable dependency went from advisory to a fixed production deploy in 35 minutes with no human step. In another, a bad release was rolled back in 3.3 seconds.

Most Environmentally Impactful ($5,000): Memory Lane

Memory Lane by Oliver McBride helps care-home coordinators build reminiscence sessions for residents with dementia. A coordinator files a plain-English issue, and three GitLab Duo flows carry it through safety review, CI/CD, and Cloud Run to production. The team measured the carbon cost of each shipped request using the Software Carbon Intensity spec, then re-engineered the pipeline to build once and skip needless runs. That cut CI-per-shipped requests by 48%.

Most Creative ($4,000): CodeTinder

CodeTinder wins in this category, too. Swiping to teach agents your taste in code was the highest-scoring idea across both paths.

What we learned

The winners kept agents on a short leash and still got a lot out of them. Agents handled the reading, writing, and routing: working out what an upgrade would break, tracing a bug to the line of code behind it, and handing the work to the next step. Automated checks like tests and CI decide whether each step passes, and, in most projects, a person signs off before anything risky ships. The winners also aimed their agents at problems outside typical software work, including pharmacy apps, benefits systems, care homes, and blind students’ classrooms.

Keep building

To everyone who entered, thank you. Thank you also to our judges: Bill Staples, Missy Davies, Mattias Michaux, Lee Tickett, Rajesh Agadi, Luca Chun Lun Lit, Alan Zhang, Jackson Dolphin, and Arianna Haradon.

title: Agentic engineering with GitLab and your local agent: A walkthrough

You can build an agentic engineering environment to drive greater automation throughout your workflow. How? Start in the harness you already use and connect to GitLab Duo Agent Platform once with a skill. Longer, repository-aware workflows run on GitLab, and every merge request still hits the same reviews, pipelines, scans, and approval policies.

In this article, we will show you how to quickly get started, from setup to tackling four key use cases. We focus on Claude Code as the local harness because that’s what we see most of our customers using but this same flow can apply to the local harness of your choosing, including Duo CLI.

How to configure your agentic engineering environment

If you already do most of your coding in a local harness, keep working there and wire it to GitLab Duo Agent Platform. From the terminal, you can direct lifecycle work to agentic workflows that run inside GitLab:

  • Picking up an issue and opening a merge request
  • Reviewing every MR as it lands
  • Resolving merge conflicts
  • Repairing a pipeline that just failed
  • With GitLab Ultimate, triaging and fixing security findings once code lands

Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, and others become the place from where you direct that work.

Part 1 is the setup

Install the GitLab Duo setup skill, ask Claude Code to run it, and it sets up your whole top-level group with the necessary settings, the flows, an automation in every project, and the MCP connection.

Part 2 walks through four workflows

You can try them as soon as the setup is done, each driven from Claude Code:

  1. Find an issue assigned to you and hand it to the Developer flow.
  2. Get automated code reviews on your merge requests, act on the findings without leaving your harness, and resolve any conflicts that pop up.
  3. Use an automation to fix a failed pipeline.
  4. On Ultimate, triage and fix security findings with the security flows.

When you want an even tighter loop

The MR followup skill guides your local harness through the steps above even faster. The skill helps local agents monitor progress on the repo-side and take actions on your behalf to speed things along.

What you need before you start

  • A GitLab.com top-level group with GitLab Credits (Premium and Ultimate groups get access to promotional free credits each month for each user). The security workflow in Use Case 4 requires Ultimate licensing for your GitLab instance.
  • A project in that group with a pipeline, a few open issues, and an open merge request or two, so the workflows have something to act on.
  • The Owner role on the top-level group, so the skill can set up the whole group. If you're a Maintainer on the project but not a group owner, the skill sets up just that project and lists what to ask your Owner.
  • Claude Code installed and signed in, plus git and the GitLab CLI (glab, signed in with glab auth login ), which the skill uses to read and change settings.

Part 1: Guided setup with a skill

The GitLab Duo setup skill accelerates the connection from inside your harness. You install the skill once, ask Claude Code to set up GitLab Duo. The skill sets up your group as it turns on group-wide Duo Agent Platform workflows, creates the Fix CI/CD Pipeline automation where needed, connects to GitLab MCP server, and reports anything left for you to finish.

Install the skill

git clone https://gitlab.com/gitlab-da/projects/agentic-eng-config.git

cp -R agentic-eng-config/skills/gitlab-duo-setup ~/.claude/skills/

cp -R agentic-eng-config/skills/gitlab-mr-followup ~/.claude/skills/

Then Claude Code picks it up in the running session. If it isn't listed, restart Claude Code. You can add the skill to .claude/skills/ inside the repo so teammates can use it too.

Run the skill

In your project directory, start Claude Code and invoke the skill with a slash command:

/gitlab-duo-setup

Note: Different harnesses can have a different syntax for invoking skills.

What happens

Before it changes anything, the skill reads your top-level group and its projects and shows you one plan: every change and what it covers (the groups or projects). Group changes reach every downstream project and every member, and the plan says so. It waits for your yes, and you can drop any line. Then it:

  1. Turns on GitLab Duo Agent Platform and flow execution for the group, and adds the Code Review, Duo Developer, and Fix CI/CD Pipeline flows to the group's flows. Flows you already have stay on.
  2. Turns on automatic code review for the group, which carries down to every project.
  3. Creates an automation in every project with CI/CD that runs Fix CI/CD Pipeline when a pipeline fails. Projects that already have one are skipped, so running the skill twice is safe.
  4. Adds the GitLab MCP server to Claude Code, user-level or project-level as you prefer, and walks you through signing in in the browser.
  5. Verifies by calling list_duo_agents_and_flows. A successful call proves the sign-in worked, and the flows it returns prove the settings took.
  6. On Ultimate, asks one optional question: Do you also want GitLab to triage and fix security findings? Say "yes" and Use Case 4 will cover what gets turned on. Say "no" and the setup is done.
  7. Ends with a short report and links for anything it couldn't do. Blockers may be runners, if a project has none that can run flows, or push rules, if your group enforces them.

Why use a skill for setup

A skill sets things up in the same place you already direct agent work. You stay in your preferred coding harness, approve a plan, and wire Duo Agent Platform for group-wide automation without breaking out of that loop.

It's also harness-neutral by design (the repo's AGENTS.md requires it), so the same skill works whether your team is on Claude Code today and something else next quarter.

If the GitLab tools don't show up

Run /mcp and check that GitLab shows as connected. Connected but no tools? Restart Claude Code; new servers load at session start.

A 403 when you sign in usually means MCP client access is off for your top-level group: A group Owner turns on Allow connection to GitLab under the group's Settings > General > Permissions and group features. If two GitLab entries, user and project scope, show duplicate tools, keep one.

Part 2: Four workflows, all run from your terminal

With the GitLab MCP server connected in Part 1, Claude Code can now find your issues, start a flow, read review threads and pipeline status, and reply on a thread over that single OAuth connection. Server instructions help Claude Code propose the right agentic workflow within Duo Agent Platform, and each call comes with an AI audit event for your platform team.

The agent reads issues and merge request context through these tools, allowing the coding harness to access GitLab artifacts you trust.

Use Case 1: Hand an issue to the Developer flow

The first thing most people want from an agent is simple: Take the issue I was assigned this morning and come back with a merge request.

Find the work

In Claude Code, ask something like:

What issues are assigned to me in ? Summarize each in a line.

Claude calls the GitLab MCP server's work item tools, filters your assignments, and gives you the list. You pick one. If the issue is thin, this is also where you'd ask Claude to read the linked files or recent commits through the repository tools so you can sharpen the description before handing it off; a clearer goal produces a better MR.

Hand it off

Ask Claude to assign the Developer flow to an issue.

Can you pick up Issue 1 and assign it to the Developer flow in GitLab?

Claude calls the server's Start Duo session tool with the project, the Developer flow, and a goal it writes from the issue, and hands you back a session link.

From here the work happens in GitLab, not on your machine. This frees you up to keep working locally without disrupting the agent. The session runs as a CI job on a runner. The flow reads the issue and the repository, writes the change, and opens a merge request. The MR is attributed to you, not to the service account, so it shows up in your activity and your review queue like any other MR you authored.

Use Case 2: Automated code review

From the harness, open or push an MR and let Duo Agent Platform review it on GitLab. You read findings and iterate locally while the review and verification stay on the merge request. GitLab Code Review flow reviews every merge request in your group as soon as the MR is marked ready. Once turned on, it enables agentic reviews and approvals.

On new groups and projects, Code Review flow is on by default, so those features are active out of the box. On existing groups and projects, you can run the setup skill to turn it on.

To check or change it for one project, go to Settings > Merge requests > GitLab Duo Code Review > Enable automatic reviews by GitLab Duo. There you can also choose to Start a new review on push so every commit to the MR branch gets a follow-up review that builds on the earlier one.

What a review looks like

When you or your agent creates an MR, GitLab Duo is added as a reviewer and runs a two-stage review: a pre-scan that pulls related files, tests and dependencies from the repo, then the review itself. It leaves inline threads with specific, actionable findings plus a summary.

With the beta approvals setting (also on the project's Merge requests settings page) turned on, GitLab Duo approves the MR when it finds nothing or requests changes when it does.

Tune it for your repo

Two files let you shape reviews without touching settings: mr-review-instructions.yaml for custom review instructions (focus areas, standards, per-path rules) and .gitlab/duo/mr-review-automated-rules.yaml to exclude MRs by target branch, source branch, or author, for example, bot-authored dependency bumps. As you identify improvements, keep updating these instructions to make reviews more efficient over time.

Work the feedback locally

Ask your agent:

Does MR 1 have feedback for me to review?

Claude Code reads Duo's Code Review threads through the MCP Server and summarizes them for you. You can ask it to follow through by fixing the ones it agrees with and reply in the threads to resolve them. Claude will make those changes locally, push them, and comment on each thread as the user. If you have the start a new review on push setting turned on, Duo will run another review to verify those changes. If a finding comes with a code suggestion, you can apply via MCP.

Long-running agentic work and verification stay on the merge request. Quick iteration stays in your local checkout.

Resolve a merge conflict

While a merge request waits for review, its target branch keeps moving. Eventually, this can lead to a conflict on your branch. You can clear it from Claude Code in two ways.

  1. Let Claude resolve it in your checkout: MR 1 conflicts with its target branch. Resolve the conflict and get the pipeline green.
  2. Or hand it over to Duo Developer on GitLab: MR 1 has a merge conflict. Can you ask the Developer flow in GitLab to resolve it?

If you use Claude Code to resolve it, it will go through the conflict locally and use any preferences in your Agents.MD or skills to resolve it. If you use GitLab Duo Developer flow, you can leave it to work on it within your GitLab instance and move on to your next task.

Use Case 3: Fix a failed pipeline with an automation

From the harness you can watch the merge request, while Duo Agent Platform can start the automated Fix CI/CD Pipeline flow when a job fails, with the same repo context and merge gates as any other change.

An automation watches for a failed pipeline and starts the Fix CI/CD Pipeline flow for you. By the time you notice the pipeline failure, a fix is usually already waiting.

Check the automation

Automations live at AI > Automations in each project. If you ran the skill, the fixed pipeline automation will already be there, along with some other automations that come out of the box. To create one by hand (Maintainer or Owner):

  1. Select New automation and give it a name, for example Fix failed pipelines.
  2. Under Runs with, select Fix CI/CD Pipeline. (Developer is selected by default if it's enabled; change it.)
  3. Under Runs when, select Add trigger > On an event, choose Pipeline events, and under Run when select Failed.
  4. Select Add event, then Create.

What happens on a failure

When a pipeline fails, the flow starts a session. If the pipeline belongs to an open merge request, it posts a system note on the MR with a link to the session. It reads the job logs, the MR diff, and the repository, then:

  • If the fix is inside the MR's diff, it applies inline code suggestions on the source branch. You review and apply them from the MR, or pull the branch and apply them locally.
  • If the fix needs files outside the diff, or the pipeline has no open MR, it opens a new merge request with the change.
  • If it can't determine a reliable fix, or the failure is security-sensitive, it posts a comment that describes the failure and next steps so you can decide how to proceed.

Make it fit your project

The flow reads AGENTS.md, so you can tell it how to format commit messages, which labels to put on MRs it opens, how to treat specific failure classes, and when to stop retrying the same fix. One known limit: The flow sees only the last 150 KiB of a job log, so noisy jobs may need a summary step at the end.

Close the loop from Claude Code

The flow leaves a system note and its suggestions on the MR, so start from the MR.

On MR 17, did Fix Pipeline create a new MR or leave suggestions? Show me the diff and the reasoning.

Decide whether to merge the MR or apply the suggestions. The MR followup skill can also help you take the MR all the way to merge and guide you through the process.

/gitlab-mr-followup Take MR 1 through to merge.

Use Case 4: Triage and fix security findings (Ultimate)

For GitLab Ultimate + Duo Agent Platform users, three out-of-the-box agents can also help eliminate security debt that builds up once code lands: Secret False Positive Detection, SAST False Positive Detection, and Resolve SAST Vulnerability. These security flows take findings from your scanners, score them for false positives, and open merge requests that fix the real ones. The flows work on findings from scans of your default branch (and other tracked branches), after code has merged.

Turn it on

If you said yes to the setup skill's security question, the skill then:

  • Adds the SAST False Positive Detection, Secret Detection False Positive Detection, and Resolve SAST Vulnerability flows to the group, keeping every flow you already have.
  • Applies the Secret Detection and SAST scan profile to projects that don't scan yet, without editing any .gitlab-ci.yml. The scans run in merge request pipelines, so if your tests only run in branch pipelines, check that a failing test still blocks the merge request.
  • Enables the flows to run the Standard preset: triage and fixes run automatically after every scan, for Medium findings and above, with up to 15 open fix merge requests per project.

If anything in this step fails, the skill stops there and leaves the setup from Part 1 as it is. Credits scale with the number of findings, so if you'd rather see results and cost first, ask for the Conservative preset when the skill shows its plan: on demand, for High and Critical findings, with at most five open fix merge requests.

Automated resolution out-of-the-box

After turning these on, agents will flag SAST and Secrets false positives for you and generate merge requests to address SAST vulnerabilities automatically, reducing your time spent on security. Expect triage and the first fix MR about 10 minutes after the scan finishes.

The Security Review flow and the Vulnerability Context flow can help you dig deeper into findings that aren’t automatically addressed.

Review before you merge

Treat the agent-created MRs like any other. You can use the Code Review flow on the fix MRs too. Security Review, which reviews merge request changes for business logic vulnerabilities, is also available. The skill mentions it but sets it up only if you ask, because it needs experiment and beta features turned on for the whole group.

Take your agentic engineering to the next level

Advanced governance, flexible model deployment, and comprehensive lifecycle context ensure your automated software factory remains secure, adaptable, and fully informed.

Governance that applies to every merge request

To ensure control and compliance as agents take on writing more code, it’s important to build guardrails that live alongside your code. Merge request approval policies, pipeline execution policies, composite identity, and tool approval guardrails apply to agent-authored changes the same way they apply to yours.

Model and cloud choice that stays under your control

GitLab Duo Agent Platform is cloud-, agent-, and model-neutral. Group owners choose the model for each agent and flow, from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and open-weight providers, and can update it as new models arrive. On GitLab Self-Managed, GitLab Duo Self-Hosted runs models through Amazon Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, or the organization’s own infrastructure.

Lifecycle context that cuts agent retries

An agent working one merge request sees only that merge request: the diff, the failing job log, and the review comments. It can't see that the same job fails in other projects. It can't see which services depend on the code it just changed, or who owns them. Without the full lifecycle picture, agents guess, then retry, then burn tokens on work that never ships.

GitLab Orbit, now generally available, is a context graph of the software lifecycle. It connects code, merge requests, work items, pipelines, vulnerabilities, and ownership, with your permissions intact. Agents get that context before they call a change safe to merge.

Developers and agents can also see which services, jobs, and environments a change touches across the group. In GitLab's internal testing, agents connected to Orbit needed up to 45x fewer retries while discovering an answer, and used up to 4.5x fewer tokens on the same tasks with the same model.

Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other MCP-compatible agents connect to Orbit through MCP or the GitLab CLI, so the context you build once serves every agent you add.

One governed path from code to production

With this integration, customers keep the coding harness their teams already use and enable GitLab Duo Agent Platform on the path to production. From the same terminal, they can turn issues into merge requests, get automated review on every MR, clear merge conflicts, let a failed pipeline start its own fix, and clear their security backlog. Every change still hits the same identity, policy, CI pipelines, security, approvals, and audit rules that their organization already trusts.

The GitLab Duo setup skill is how that connection starts. Install it in your harness, invoke it once, and review a single plan before anything changes. After you approve, the skill turns on Duo Agent Platform for your group, adds the Code Review, Fix CI/CD Pipeline, and Developer flows, creates the failed-pipeline automation where it is needed, connects the GitLab MCP server, and verifies the sign-in. It ends with a short report and links for anything left for you or your group Owner. From there, the four workflows in this guide run from the same terminal, and the MR followup skill is available when you want the loop even tighter.

New to GitLab Duo Agent Platform? Start a free trial. Already on Premium or Ultimate? Turn on Duo Agent Platform and use the GitLab Credits included with your subscription. Then clone the GitLab Duo setup skill, run it from the harness you already use, and take the first workflow for a spin on a real project.

Hand it off

Ask Claude to assign the Developer flow to an issue.

Can you pick up Issue 1 and assign it to the Developer flow in GitLab?

Claude calls the server's Start Duo session tool with the project, the Developer flow, and a goal it writes from the issue, and hands you back a session link.

From here the work happens in GitLab, not on your machine. This frees you up to keep working locally without disrupting the agent. The session runs as a CI job on a runner. The flow reads the issue and the repository, writes the change, and opens a merge request. The MR is attributed to you, not to the service account, so it shows up in your activity and your review queue like any other MR you authored.

Use Case 2: Automated code review

From the harness, open or push an MR and let Duo Agent Platform review it on GitLab. You read findings and iterate locally while the review and verification stay on the merge request. GitLab Code Review flow reviews every merge request in your group as soon as the MR is marked ready. Once turned on, it enables agentic reviews and approvals.

On new groups and projects, Code Review flow is on by default, so those features are active out of the box. On existing groups and projects, you can run the setup skill to turn it on.

To check or change it for one project, go to Settings > Merge requests > GitLab Duo Code Review > Enable automatic reviews by GitLab Duo. There you can also choose to Start a new review on push so every commit to the MR branch gets a follow-up review that builds on the earlier one.

What a review looks like

When you or your agent creates an MR, GitLab Duo is added as a reviewer and runs a two-stage review: a pre-scan that pulls related files, tests and dependencies from the repo, then the review itself. It leaves inline threads with specific, actionable findings plus a summary.

With the beta approvals setting (also on the project's Merge requests settings page) turned on, GitLab Duo approves the MR when it finds nothing or requests changes when it does.

Tune it for your repo

Two files let you shape reviews without touching settings: mr-review-instructions.yaml for custom review instructions (focus areas, standards, per-path rules) and .gitlab/duo/mr-review-automated-rules.yaml to exclude MRs by target branch, source branch, or author, for example, bot-authored dependency bumps. As you identify improvements, keep updating these instructions to make reviews more efficient over time.

Work the feedback locally

Ask your agent:

Does MR 1 have feedback for me to review?

Claude Code reads Duo's Code Review threads through the MCP Server and summarizes them for you. You can ask it to follow through by fixing the ones it agrees with and reply in the threads to resolve them. Claude will make those changes locally, push them, and comment on each thread as the user. If you have the start a new review on push setting turned on, Duo will run another review to verify those changes. If a finding comes with a code suggestion, you can apply via MCP.

Long-running agentic work and verification stay on the merge request. Quick iteration stays in your local checkout.

While a merge request waits for review, its target branch keeps moving. Eventually, this can lead to a conflict on your branch. You can clear it from Claude Code in two ways.

  1. Let Claude resolve it in your checkout: MR 1 conflicts with its target branch. Resolve the conflict and get the pipeline green.
  2. Or hand it over to Duo Developer on GitLab: MR 1 has a merge conflict. Can you ask the Developer flow in GitLab to resolve it?

From the harness you can watch the merge request, while Duo Agent Platform can start the automated Fix CI/CD Pipeline flow when a job fails, with the same repo context and merge gates as any other change.

  2. Under Runs with, select Fix CI/CD Pipeline. (Developer is selected by default if it's enabled; change it.)

  • If the fix is inside the MR's diff, it applies inline code suggestions on the source branch. You review and apply them from the MR, or pull the branch and apply them locally.
  • If the fix needs files outside the diff, or the pipeline has no open MR, it opens a new merge request with the change.
  • If it can't determine a reliable fix, or the failure is security-sensitive, it posts a comment that describes the failure and next steps so you can decide how to proceed.

Make it fit your project

The flow reads AGENTS.md, so you can tell it how to format commit messages, which labels to put on MRs it opens, how to treat specific failure classes, and when to stop retrying the same fix. Close the loop from Claude Code

The flow leaves a system note and its suggestions on the MR, so start from the MR.

On MR 17, did Fix Pipeline create a new MR or leave suggestions? Show me the diff and the reasoning.

Decide whether to merge the MR or apply the suggestions. The MR followup skill can also help you take the MR all the way to merge and guide you through the process.

/gitlab-mr-followup Take MR 1 through to merge.

Use Case 4: Triage and fix security findings (Ultimate)

For GitLab Ultimate + Duo Agent Platform users, three out-of-the-box agents can also help eliminate security debt that builds up once code lands: Secret False Positive Detection, SAST False Positive Detection, and Resolve SAST Vulnerability.
